strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with rigorous ablations, statistical significance testing, and detailed analysis of training dynamics across multiple strategies (PPO, DAgger, EarlySwitcher, EALM)
Strong empirical results achieving 40.1% SR on unseen categories without depth/odometry, matching or exceeding methods with additional sensors, while being lightweight (130M parameters, RGB-only)

Excellent reproducibility with comprehensive hyperparameter tables, training curves, loss component analysis, and promised code release enabling replication

Critical dependence on segmentation quality with 43% relative performance drop (70.4% to 40.1% SR) between ground-truth and predicted masks; Table 11 shows complete breakdown (0.1% SR) without masks, questioning practical applicability

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations, statistical significance testing, and detailed appendix supporting reproducibility

Strong performance on HM3D-OVON benchmark meeting or exceeding several baselines when using ground-truth masks
Thorough reproducibility materials including promised code release and complete hyperparameters
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation: Method fundamentally depends on ground-truth binary segmentation masks at test time. Table 4 reveals catastrophic performance degradation—from 70.4% SR with GT masks to 35.5% with predicted YOLOE segmentation (~50% absolute drop)—which directly contradicts practical applicability claims and is not adequately addressed in the main paper

Unfair experimental comparison: Table 1 results use ground-truth masks for OVSegDT while baselines (DAgRL, Uni-NaVid) lack this privileged information. On val seen, OVSegDT (41.0%) actually underperforms DAgRL (41.3%), undermining the SOTA claim when adjusting for this confound

Limited conceptual novelty: Three contributions are straightforward engineering—binary mask encoder via ResNet9 is standard, auxiliary segmentation loss is well-established multi-task learning, and EALM is simple linear interpolation between losses ($\lambda_t = \text{clip}(\frac{H_{\text{high}} - \hat{H}_t}{H_{\text{high}} - H_{\text{low}}}, 0, 1)$) without principled justification

Auxiliary segmentation loss creates unexplained trade-offs: Adding L_seg increases success rate modestly (+1.1%, Table 3) but worsens SPL (40.8→39.4) and increases collisions by 30% (14.5→18.8), yet is retained without adequate justification beyond subjective metric prioritization

Missing critical hyperparameter ablations: Entropy bounds (0.35, 0.75) are presented without sensitivity analysis or justification. Per-category confidence threshold calibration (Figs. 6-7) requires manual tuning that doesn't scale, contradicting claims of principled design

Severely limited evaluation scope: Single benchmark (HM3D-OVON), simulation-only with no real-world deployment or sim-to-real analysis, no failure case analysis, and no investigation of performance across object categories or environmental conditions

Inconsistent and contradictory reporting: Unclear separation between results with GT masks (70.4% SR) versus predicted segmentation (40.1% SR), making it ambiguous what the main contribution represents. Claims about avoiding 'large vision-language models' are misleading given reliance on pre-trained SigLIP and YOLOE

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations (Tables 2-4) and collision count analysis as safety metric

Principled EALM approach provides automatic, entropy-based loss scheduling that eliminates brittle manual phase switching, with clear empirical validation in Table 2
Lightweight method (130M parameters, RGB-only) that outperforms methods with additional sensors (depth/odometry) on the val unseen split

weaknesses: Critical dependence on segmentation masks: Table 3 reveals that the goal mask accounts for ~49 percentage point performance gain (20.2% to 69.3% SR), dwarfing contributions from EALM and auxiliary loss alone. Limited algorithmic novelty: Mixing losses based on entropy is relatively straightforward; auxiliary segmentation tasks are established techniques. Contribution is primarily in application combination rather than fundamental innovation

Incomplete technical justification: No ablation on ResNet9 choice for mask encoder. Table 11 shows complete failure without masks (0.1% SR), indicating text embeddings are largely decorative for unseen categories despite claims of multi-modal grounding

Remaining data bottleneck unaddressed: Despite 33% sample efficiency improvement, method requires 200M training steps on only 216 scenes. Generalization to environments beyond HM3D and to novel object categories outside training vocabulary remains unclear
No real robot experiments or validation of sim-to-real transferability. All evaluation confined to simulation with manual calibration requirements that may not scale
Missing key comparisons: No comparison with other segmentation-aware methods. Limited analysis of category-specific performance and failure modes. No inference time/memory comparisons with baselines
Code availability incomplete: Promised code link missing (shown as '.' in submission), limiting reproducibility claims despite comprehensive methodology description

strengths: Strong empirical results with thorough experimental validation: 44.7% SR on HM3D-OVON unseen categories outperforming larger models (Uni-NaVid, TANGO), supported by comprehensive ablations and statistical significance testing

Comprehensive experimental methodology: Extensive ablations isolating component contributions, entropy threshold analysis (Appendix C), failure analysis (Table 5), statistical significance testing, and real robot demonstration
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-organized paper with informative visualizations, complete hyperparameter specifications in appendix, and detailed training dynamics analysis
weaknesses: Critical segmentation dependency with substantial performance cliff: 69.3% SR with ground-truth masks drops to 28.8% with raw YOLOE predictions, then recovers to 44.7% only after manual per-category confidence calibration—this 24.6 percentage point gap severely limits real-world applicability

Semantic reward uses ground-truth mask area at inference time (Eq. 4), creating train-test mismatch and undermining end-to-end learning claims; auxiliary segmentation loss increases collisions (45.4 vs 29.4) without adequate investigation of this safety-performance trade-off

Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing components (SigLIP [38], transformer [38], DCGAN). Binary goal mask input acknowledged as prior work (PixelNav). EALM is the main novel contribution but is relatively straightforward entropy-weighted interpolation

Generalization claims overstated: 'Unseen categories' remain within HM3D simulator's visual distribution; no cross-environment (AI2-Thor, ProcTHOR) or cross-dataset evaluation. Real robot experiments limited to 2 demonstrations with different camera FoV (105° vs 42°), not true sim-to-real transfer

Two-stage training protocol deviates from end-to-end: 200M steps with ground-truth masks followed by 15M with predicted masks. Requires manual per-category threshold calibration that doesn't scale. Unclear if hyperparameters generalize beyond HM3D

Evaluation limited to single benchmark: Only HM3D-OVON assessment with no cross-benchmark validation. Insufficient real-world validation with acknowledged 'risky behavior near goal' due to reward design

EALM hyperparameter justification incomplete: Entropy bounds derived heuristically; EMA coefficient α=0.95 unjustified; sensitivity analysis limited to Appendix C only. Generalization to different action spaces unclear

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation with thorough ablations, statistical significance testing, and failure analysis demonstrating rigorous evaluation methodology
EALM provides an effective and well-motivated solution to the brittle manual phase-switching problem in DAgger-PPO pipelines, with clear empirical benefits (10% collision reduction)
Strong empirical results on HM3D-OVON benchmark (44.7% SR, 20.6% SPL unseen) achieving SOTA while using lightweight architecture (130M params) with only RGB input
Well-executed paper with practical considerations: efficient inference on edge devices, transparency about limitations, and real robot demonstrations
Clear problem formulation and good qualitative analysis (Figure 3, Table 5) providing interpretability of when and why the method works or fails
weaknesses: Critical reliance on privileged information: ground-truth segmentation masks during training (69.3% SR) vs. predicted segmentation at test time (28.8% SR gap); semantic reward (Eq. 4) uses ground-truth mask area unavailable at deployment, creating train-test mismatch that undermines end-to-end learning claims

Misleading framing of generalization: Claims to be 'first to show' generalization to unseen categories, but this largely emerges from the external YOLOE segmentation model, not the learned policy. Binary masks provided as input are not purely 'RGB input'

Limited architectural and methodological novelty: Transformer backbone is from prior work, goal mask encoder is simple ResNet9, EALM is straightforward entropy-based loss mixing (Eq. 6) lacking technical depth

Unfair experimental comparisons: (1) Different training budgets (DAgRL: 300M vs. OVSegDT: 200M), (2) OVSegDT receives binary mask input while baselines don't—a substantial information advantage not clearly acknowledged, (3) Inconsistent error bars across methods

Narrow evaluation scope severely limiting generalization claims: Only HM3D-OVON benchmark tested; no evaluation on other simulators; real-world validation limited to 2 demonstration scenarios; acknowledged 'risky behavior near goal' when deployed; no transfer learning experiments

Training complexity contradicts 'single-stage' claims: 200M steps ground-truth pretraining + 15M predicted segmentation fine-tuning + per-category confidence calibration + manual vocabulary curation suggests heavy task-specific tuning rather than general approach

Methodological concerns: (1) Semantic reward uses unavailable ground-truth information at test time, (2) Detector confidence calibration per category suggests misalignment, (3) 61.3% false negative rate in Table 5 indicates segmentation errors critically degrade performance but isn't adequately addressed, (4) Entropy threshold selection (Eqs. 5-6) lacks theoretical justification despite ablation

Missing critical comparisons and ablations: No comparison to PixelNav which also uses segmentation masks; no ablation removing ground-truth mask pretraining; unclear performance when baselines also receive mask input; only 3 random seeds; real robot uses different camera setup (105° vs 42° FoV)

strengths: Strong empirical results: Achieves SOTA on HM3D-OVON (44.7% SR, 20.6% SPL on val unseen) using only RGB input with lightweight 130M parameter model, outperforming larger models like Uni-NaVid (43.9%) and TANGO (35.5%)

Novel EALM contribution: Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation elegantly solves the brittle DAgger→PPO phase switching problem using policy entropy as continuous uncertainty signal; well-motivated choice of entropy bounds grounded in action space analysis; general technique applicable beyond this task
Exceptional generalization: Nearly identical performance on seen (43.6%) vs unseen (44.7%) categories demonstrates robust learning of generalizable representations despite limited training data

Comprehensive experimental validation: Rigorous ablation studies (Tables 2-5), statistical significance testing (Appendix F), sensitivity analysis for entropy thresholds (Appendix C), and detailed loss component evolution; failure analysis (Table 5) provides actionable insights

Pragmatic sim-to-real strategy: Addresses realistic challenge of unavailable ground-truth segmentation through per-category confidence calibration and fine-tuning, with analysis showing FNR reduction as key improvement mechanism

Clear presentation with extensive reproducibility details: Detailed hyperparameter tables (Appendices A-C), informative architecture figures, and complete loss formulations enabling verification of claims
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on external segmentation model: 2.4× performance cliff without ground-truth (69.3% SR with GT vs 28.8% with YOLOE), indicating tight coupling to segmentation quality; requires manual per-category confidence threshold tuning (0.01-0.4 range); fundamental limitation that reduces independence of navigation contribution

Limited architectural novelty: Architecture largely follows DagRL [38] with frozen SigLIP encoders; goal mask encoding uses standard ResNet9; main novelty is EALM training procedure rather than architectural innovation

Narrow evaluation scope: Single benchmark (HM3D-OVON) only; no experiments on AI2-THOR, ProcTHOR, or other datasets; real-world validation limited to 2 demonstration scenarios on single robot type with acknowledged sim-to-real safety gap ('risky behavior near goal'); indoor navigation only

Insufficient justification for auxiliary segmentation loss: Connection to 'learning effective representations' is speculative; loss is 1-2 orders of magnitude smaller than policy losses (Appendix E, Figure J) suggesting minor contribution; unclear why reconstruction loss is necessary when model only uses masks as input

Heuristic entropy bounds lack generalization validation: Entropy thresholds (0.35, 0.75) chosen through heuristic despite principled motivation; Appendix C tests only 3 configurations; proposed generalization rules (H_high ∈ [0.4,0.5]·log|A|) lack validation on alternative domains/action spaces; EMA parameter α=0.95 appears arbitrary

Extreme computational requirements limit reproducibility: 200M+15M training steps on 2 A100 GPUs with 40 parallel environments; sample efficiency gains claimed (33% reduction) lack clear baseline specification; inaccessible to most researchers

Limited theoretical justification for EALM: Intuitive but lacks formal justification for why entropy should indicate readiness to transition from IL to RL; no comparison with alternative information-theoretic criteria; entropy can reflect exploration OR uncertainty without distinguishing cases

Persistent major failure modes: Goal recognition (28.2%) and reaching (18.2%) failures remain significant (Table 5); high FNR (61.3%) in segmentation suggests continued struggles with distant/occluded objects; limited discussion of remediation pathways
